dih.f: (African-American Vernacular, euphemistic, Internet slang, humorous, mildly vulgar) Filter-avoidance spelling of dick.

s.g: (mathematics) An angle between two plane surfaces
(aeronautics) The upward slope of an aircraft's wing
(chemistry) The angle between pairs of chemical bonds separated by a third bond
(mathematics) Consisting of, relating to or contained between two plane surfaces.
(of a kite or an aeroplane) Having wings that form a dihedral angle, especially when the angle between the upper sides is less than 180°.
(aviation) Of wing pairs, inclined at an upward angle to each other.
(chemistry) A hydrate whose solid contains two molecules of water of crystallization per molecule, or per unit cell
(chemistry, especially in combination) Two hydrogen atoms in a molecule
(chemistry) Any hydrochloride formed by reaction with two molecules of hydrochloric acid
(pharmacology) A particular narcotic painkiller.
Any salt or ester of dihydrofolic acid
(chemistry) The divalent radical formed from two separate hydrogen atoms or ions.
(chemistry, modifying a noun) Describing a dihydrogen bond.
(inorganic chemistry) The diatomic hydrogen molecule H₂.
A molecule based upon pyridine, the parent of a class of molecules that have been semi-saturated with two substituents replacing one double bond.
(organic chemistry) The chromenone (2R,3R)-2-(3,4-dihydroxyphenyl)-3,5,7-trihydroxy-2,3-dihydrochromen-4-one
(organic chemistry) The dihydro derivative of rhodamine which is converted to the fluorescent parent compound in the presence of a reactive oxygen species
(biochemistry) An androgenic metabolite of testosterone; used to treat certain breast cancers.
(chemistry) Containing two hydroxy functional groups.
(organic chemistry) The compound CO(CH₂OH)₂ that has a number of industrial uses.
(biochemistry) The only ketotriose.
A physiologically active metabolite of a vitamin, with two hydroxy groups substituted in any position.
